blocks.text: …the event was canceled by the contract holder because of fraud! Fraud! In front of everyone!"
I put her on speaker so my fiancée, Emma, could hear. "The guard is right," I said calmly. "You called the venue pretending to be Emma. That's what the coordinator called it, too."
There was a long silence. Then her mother, Diane, started crying and said I'd humiliated her in front of all her friends. Emma took the phone out of my hand.
"Mom," she said quietly, "you canceled my wedding three weeks before it happened and told me to get married at the courthouse. You don't get to be the one who's humiliated."
It was the first time I'd ever heard Emma stand up to her mother. Her hands were shaking afterward, but she said it felt like breathing for the first time in years.
It turned out Diane had told the venue that "her daughter" had decided to cancel the wedding and wanted to move the deposit to a family anniversary gala that Friday instead.

Because the coordinator had never spoken with Emma, she believed it. When I called on Monday with the contract and my card statement, the coordinator was mortified. She restored our wedding date, canceled the gala, and flagged our file so no one could make changes without speaking to me in person.

Diane had never told her guests about the switch. She'd planned to announce at a family brunch that she'd "found a better venue" for her party. So sixty people drove to a locked gate, and the story spread through her friend group by Saturday morning.

For two weeks, Emma's mother refused to speak to us. Then, a week before the wedding, she showed up at our apartment with Emma's father. She apologized to Emma, and then, stiffly, to me. Emma told her she was welcome at the wedding on one condition: no surprises.
We got married at the lakeside estate on our original date. Diane sat in the front row and cried through the whole ceremony. This time, I think they were real tears.
A month after the wedding, Emma and I gave her parents a belated twenty-fifth anniversary dinner for two at the same estate. We booked it in my name.
